title: Renting as a Student in India: Your First Place Away From Home
seoTitle: Renting as a Student in India: A Guide
description: PG, hostel or a shared flat? A practical guide for students renting in India: deposits, guarantors, flatmates, campus commutes, safety and leaving well.
excerpt: No salary slip, no rental history, a small budget and owners who would rather not rent to students. Here is how to find a first place near campus without losing money or sleep.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: We all had a first room with a bad fan

hero.alt: Futuristic illustration of a compact student room with a glowing route tracing from the desk to a distant campus

faq.q: Can I rent a flat in India as a student with no income proof?
faq.a: Yes, though it takes more explaining than it does for a salaried tenant. Owners ask for income proof to reassure themselves the rent will arrive, so give them a different form of reassurance: your college ID and admission letter, a parent who speaks to them directly and signs as guarantor, and a clear statement of how long you intend to stay. Many owners are fine with a student once a parent is visibly behind the rent. Some will still say no, and that is not worth taking personally.

faq.q: Is a PG cheaper than sharing a flat?
faq.a: It depends on what you count. A PG is usually one monthly figure that already covers food, cleaning and often utilities, so it is predictable and needs less upfront money. A shared flat can work out lower per person on rent alone, but you add utilities, internet, gas, cleaning and every meal you cook, plus a much larger deposit split between you. Compare the total monthly outgoing and the total upfront payment, not the headline figures, and factor in that a flat also costs you time.

faq.q: Whose name should be on the agreement in a shared flat?
faq.a: Ideally all of yours. If only one name is on it, that person legally owes the entire rent, and when a flatmate leaves mid-year the owner will hold the named tenant responsible for the full amount. Ask the owner to name every flatmate as a co-tenant, and separately write a short signed agreement between yourselves covering shares, deposit contributions, notice, and who is responsible for finding a replacement if someone leaves early.

faq.q: Can I negotiate the deposit as a student?
faq.a: Very often, yes, and it is usually the most negotiable term in the whole arrangement. Deposits reflect the owner’s worry, so reduce the worry: offer a longer commitment, offer a couple of months’ rent in advance instead, bring a parent in as guarantor, or simply ask for a lower figure and see what comes back. In a PG, the terms are set by the operator rather than any statute, which means there is more room to move than the printed sheet suggests.

faq.q: What happens to my room and my deposit over the summer break?
faq.a: That depends entirely on what you agreed, which is why it should be settled before you move in rather than in April. Some owners will hold the room for a reduced retention charge, which can be cheaper than moving out and back. Some PGs run monthly and simply re-let the bed. If you are leaving properly, give written notice in the format the agreement specifies, do a joint walkthrough against your move-in photographs, and get the deposit settlement in writing.

There is no single national rule. Some states and municipal corporations have registration or licensing requirements for paying-guest accommodation and others have none, and the rules change, so check what applies in your own city rather than assuming. Practically, a PG bed is frequently not covered by a formal tenancy agreement at all — the terms are set by the operator. Ask for something in writing covering the amount, what it includes, the deposit and the notice period, even if it is only a signed note.

body:
The lane behind the college had four PGs in it, and Arjun saw three of them in one July afternoon, with his father waiting downstairs each time because there was nowhere to sit.

The first had a bed free by the window. Good light, a working fan, a cupboard with a door that shut. Food included, the caretaker said, and Arjun was already deciding where the laptop would go. Then his father asked the question Arjun hadn't thought to ask: what else? Two months' deposit. A one-time "joining" charge. Laundry extra. Guests not allowed past the stairs. Gate shuts at ten, and if you're later than that you call the owner, who will not be pleased.

It was still a good room. But the number in his head had been the monthly rent, and the number on the table was roughly three times that before he'd slept there one night.

That gap — between the price you're told and the money you actually need — catches almost every student out. Here's the rest of what nobody tells you.

## Why owners hesitate, and what actually gets you the room

You will meet owners who don't want to rent to you. Not personally — they've never met you. It's the category. The objections are consistent enough that you can answer them instead of being surprised by them:

- **No income proof.** The standard filter for a salaried tenant is a salary slip or a bank statement showing money arriving monthly. You have neither, and nothing you say about being reliable comes with a document.
- **No rental history.** Nobody can vouch that you paid on time somewhere else, because you've never rented anywhere.
- **The noise and damage assumptions.** Owners in buildings full of families worry about late nights and a flat that becomes everyone's hangout. Sometimes that worry is fair. Usually it isn't. It gets applied to you either way.
- **Short stay.** A student might leave when the course ends, or in the summer, or when a hostel seat opens up. Owners want eleven months, minimum.

The counter to all of it is the same: make yourself a known quantity. A parent who speaks to the owner directly. Your college ID and admission letter. A clear statement of how long you'll stay and who's paying. If it's a shared flat, introduce the flatmates rather than mentioning them vaguely — an owner who has met the people is far more relaxed than one imagining a rotating cast of strangers. And be straightforward about the money coming from home. That's how most students rent.

## PG, hostel or a shared flat?

These three get talked about as if they're versions of the same thing. They're not. They're different lives, and the right one depends more on how you want to live than on which is cheapest.

| | **PG (paying guest)** | **Hostel** | **Shared flat** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Setup** | A room, often shared 2–4 ways, run as a business | A room in a block, run by the institution or an operator | A whole flat rented by you and your flatmates |
| **Cost shape** | One monthly figure, often including food and utilities | Often a term or annual fee, mess fees sometimes separate | Rent split, plus utilities, internet, gas and everything you buy |
| **Deposit** | Usually one to a few months, set by the operator | Often a refundable caution deposit | The heaviest — the full flat deposit, split between you |
| **Food** | Commonly included; quality varies, choice rarely | Mess food, fixed timings, fixed menu | You cook, or you don't eat |
| **Privacy** | Low — possibly a room with strangers assigned to you | Low to very low | Highest; you chose who's here |
| **Rules** | Operator's: curfews, guest rules, sometimes cooking bans | Institutional, often strict | Whatever you and the owner agreed, plus building rules |
| **Chores** | Cleaning and often laundry handled | Cleaning handled | All yours |
| **Best when** | You're new to the city and want a soft landing | You want cheapest and closest to campus | You want your own life and can handle bills and people |
| **Worst when** | You need quiet, odd hours or a kitchen | You need any flexibility at all | A flatmate leaves in March |

A PG is a service, not really a tenancy — you're buying a bed and a set of arrangements. That's why it can be a good first step: you arrive in a city you don't know, and food, cleaning and a locked gate are handled while you work out where anything is.

A shared flat is a small business you run with your friends. Somebody has to remember the electricity bill. Somebody has to buy gas. When it works it's the best of the three by a distance. When a flatmate leaves in March, it's the one that can genuinely hurt you financially.

## What a PG usually includes — and what it usually doesn't

There's no standard. Every PG defines its own package, so treat the word as meaningless until someone tells you what's in it. Ask, specifically:

- **Sharing count.** Single, double, triple, four-share? A "double" that becomes a triple in September because a bed was added is a real thing that happens. Get the number in writing, even in a WhatsApp message.
- **Food.** How many meals, on what days, at what timings, and what happens if you're in a lab until nine. Fixed menu or any choice?
- **Utilities.** Electricity in the monthly figure, or metered per room and billed separately? That one catches people out badly in May.
- **Laundry, cleaning and Wi-Fi.** Included, extra, or shared with fifteen people — and does the Wi-Fi survive 11pm?
- **Curfew.** The actual time, and what happens when you're late. Some lock the gate. Some call your parents.
- **Guests.** Most limit or prohibit visitors in rooms; some don't allow them past the entrance. If friends will visit, know this on day one.
- **Cooking.** Frequently banned outright, including kettles and induction plates.
- **Notice period.** How much notice to leave, and whether it's forfeited from the deposit if you go early.

Two things worth being clear-eyed about. A PG bed is often **not** covered by a formal tenancy agreement at all — it may be a receipt, a register entry, or nothing written down, so ask for something in writing regardless. And whether PGs need any licence or registration depends on your state and city; some municipalities have rules, others have none, and they change. Don't assume protections exist. Check locally.

Because the terms are set by the operator rather than by statute, they're also more negotiable than they sound. A month's deposit instead of two, or the joining fee waived, is a normal conversation.

## Sharing a flat: flatmates, splitting, and whose name is on the agreement

This is the part students get wrong most expensively, and it's not about rent. It's about names.

**Whose name is on the agreement decides who owes the money.** If the agreement is in your name alone and two friends pay you their share informally, then legally the whole rent is yours. When one of them leaves in March because an internship came up in another city, the owner will not care. You will owe the full rent and the full remaining commitment, and you'll be chasing a friend for money over WhatsApp. Friendships have ended over less.

The safer arrangements:

1. **All tenants named on one agreement.** Everyone is on the hook, everyone has standing, and the owner can't quietly treat one of you as the only real tenant. Ask for this — many owners agree once you explain why. The [rental agreements guide](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india) covers what else belongs in it.
2. **A written side-agreement between flatmates.** Even a signed one-pager covering: who pays what share and when, who contributed how much deposit, how much notice someone must give before leaving, and — the important one — **that the person leaving finds a replacement or covers their share until one is found.** Not legally bulletproof, but it turns a fight into a reference.

On splitting fairly: rooms are rarely equal, and the one with the attached bathroom shouldn't cost the same as the box room by the kitchen. Argue about it once, on day one, rather than resentfully for eleven months. Track who paid how much of the deposit, too — when someone leaves mid-year their share comes from the incoming flatmate or from you, and without a record that conversation is guesswork.

And choose flatmates for their habits, not their company. The friend you like best isn't automatically the person you want to share a bathroom with. Sleep schedules, guests, cleaning, smoking, whether they'll actually pay on the 5th — ask directly. Less awkward now than in month four.

## The money: the deposit is what actually stops you

Rent is the number you can plan for. The deposit is the number that decides whether you can move at all, because it lands in one payment before you have keys.

Deposit norms differ wildly across Indian cities and there's no national figure — some places expect a couple of months, others a great deal more. What matters for you is this: **the deposit is very often the most negotiable term in the whole arrangement.**

Owners hold deposits partly as security and partly out of habit. Reduce the risk they're worried about and you can often reduce the number:

- Offer a longer commitment — "I'm here for two years, not one term."
- Offer a couple of months' rent in advance instead of a large deposit.
- Bring a parent in as guarantor, which addresses the underlying worry directly.
- Just ask. Ask for one month instead of three and see what comes back. The worst outcome is the original number.

Whatever you agree, get the amount, the refund timeline and the deduction rules written down — that's what goes wrong on the way out. Our [guide to security deposits in India](/blog/security-deposits-in-india) covers the refund protocol and what can legitimately be deducted.

Then budget for the whole first outlay: deposit, first month's rent (often payable together, not a month later), brokerage if you used an agent, agreement and stamp costs where applicable, any joining charge, a mattress if the room doesn't come with one, bucket and curtains and a plug board and a lock, kitchen basics if you're in a flat, and getting your stuff there.

Almost none of that recurs, which is exactly why it gets forgotten. The [hidden costs of renting in India](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india) breaks the full picture down. Do the arithmetic before you say yes, not after.

## Documents you'll be asked for, and how a parent guarantor works

Expect to be asked for some combination of:

- Photo ID (Aadhaar is the usual ask, sometimes a passport)
- College ID card and your admission or enrolment letter
- Passport photographs
- Parent's or guardian's ID and address proof
- Occasionally a parent's income proof or bank statement
- Sometimes a local reference — a relative, or someone the owner can call

A guarantor arrangement is simply your parent standing behind the rent. It takes one of three shapes: your parent signs as the tenant with you named as the occupant; you're the tenant and your parent signs a separate guarantee; or — very commonly — there's nothing formal and the owner just wants a phone number and a conversation.

If a parent is guaranteeing, make sure they know what they're agreeing to: the full monthly amount, the length of the commitment, the notice terms. Vague verbal understandings between an owner and a parent four hundred kilometres away are where misunderstandings breed.

One warning, because students get targeted for it: never pay a deposit or "booking amount" for a room you haven't seen, to someone you haven't met, on the promise that it'll be held for you. Advance-payment fraud around campuses at the start of term is common and follows a predictable script — our piece on [rental scams in India](/blog/rental-scams-in-india) walks through the patterns.

## Choosing where to live around a campus

The trap is picking purely on rent, ending up twenty minutes further out, and paying the difference back in auto fares and lost sleep every day.

Things that matter more than they look on a map:

- **Commute at the hour you actually travel.** Not Sunday afternoon. A weekday nine-in-the-morning route is a different road entirely. If you have evening labs, test the way back at that hour too.
- **The walk from wherever the bus or metro drops you.** That last stretch is the part you'll do a thousand times, often after dark. Is it lit? Is anyone else on it?
- **Food after 9pm.** Not a small thing for a student. Nothing open late means you'll spend more on delivery than you expect.
- **A shop, a chemist, somewhere to print things.** Boring, constant needs.
- **Water supply.** Ask whether tankers are normal in summer. In a shared flat, that becomes your bill.
- **Who else lives in the building.** Families have a different rhythm than a mostly-student block. Neither is wrong; they suit different people.

Walk the area once at night before you commit. Ten minutes of walking tells you more than an hour of photographs. Our [house-hunting checklist](/blog/house-hunting-checklist-india) has the general version; for a student the decisive additions are the night walk and the real-hour commute.

## Staying safe when it's your first place away from home

Practical, not paranoid:

- **Tell someone where you are.** Share the address with a parent or a friend at home, and your location with one person you trust when you're heading back late.
- **Know your lock, and who else has keys.** Owners, caretakers, cleaners — a reasonable question, and the answer tells you how the place is run. If the door has a flimsy latch, ask for it to be changed. In a shared room, check whether your cupboard locks.
- **Know a second way home** that isn't the shortcut through the dark lane, even if it's five minutes longer.
- **Keep cash and a spare key somewhere else.** Locked out at midnight is solvable if you planned for it.
- **Trust the feeling.** A knock at odd hours, entry without notice, questions that aren't anyone's business — that's information. Say it out loud to someone. Being new to a city is not a reason to be polite about something that feels wrong.
- **Emergency numbers saved**, plus one local person who could reach you in twenty minutes.

Most of that is a fifteen-minute setup you do once, in your first week rather than after something happens.

## Check the room itself before you agree

Quickly, out loud, in front of whoever is showing it:

- Turn on every light, fan and switch. Ask about the ones that don't work.
- Run the taps for pressure, and time the geyser if there is one.
- Look under the sink for leaks and at the ceiling and skirting for damp.
- Check phone signal in the room, not the corridor.
- Open and close the windows. Do they lock? Is there a grill?
- Sit still for a minute and listen — road noise, a generator, the neighbours' TV. None of that shows up in photographs.
- On move-in day, photograph every mark, stain and crack and send them to the owner. Cheapest thing you can do to protect your deposit.

The [full list of questions to ask](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting) covers what to put to the owner.

## Leaving: semesters, eleven months, and getting the deposit back

Most Indian rental agreements run eleven months. Your academic year doesn't. That mismatch is the source of most student exit problems.

Sort it out at the start:

- **If you'll leave for the summer**, say so before signing. Some owners accept a shorter term for slightly higher rent, some PGs run monthly anyway, and some will hold the room over the break for a reduced retention charge — ask, because part rent for two months may beat moving twice.
- **Check the notice period and the lock-in.** A lock-in means you owe rent for that period whether you're there or not. If your course might change, that's the clause to read.
- **In a shared flat, know what happens when one person goes.** That's what the side-agreement is for.
- **Don't leave the deposit to trust.** Give written notice in the format the agreement specifies, do a joint walkthrough before handing back keys, compare against your move-in photos, get the settlement in writing, and hand over keys against a receipt.

If you're leaving early, the [breaking a lease in India](/blog/breaking-a-lease-in-india) guide covers the notice and lock-in mechanics.

One legal note, brief because it's widely misunderstood: the Model Tenancy Act, 2021 is a *model* law and binds nobody by itself. Tenancy is a state subject, so it applies only where your state has enacted its own version, and many haven't. What governs you is your state's rent legislation and the agreement you actually signed. If you're relying on a rule you read online, check whether your state adopted it.

## Where StayOnMap fits

Short version, because you've got enough to read.

The homepage is a map, so you can look at the area around your campus before you look at any rooms — which is the right order for a student, given that the commute and the walk back at night matter more than the photographs do.

PG listings state the sharing count and bed availability as structured fields, so you can see whether a room is a double or a four-share without messaging anyone. Rent, deposit and maintenance are required fields on every listing, so the real number is visible before you get attached to a room.

There's no brokerage, which matters most when the budget is smallest. And you contact the owner directly, so the first conversation about the deposit is with the person who can actually change it.

## Before you say yes

- You know the total first payment, not just the rent
- You've asked what the deposit covers and tried to negotiate it
- You know the notice period, any lock-in, and the curfew and guest rules
- You've seen the room at a realistic hour and photographed its condition
- You've walked the route back at night
- Somebody at home has the address and the owner's number
- Shared flat: names on the agreement sorted, and a written split between flatmates
- You have something in writing, even if it's short

Your first place doesn't have to be the perfect place. It has to be one that doesn't cost you money or sleep you can't spare. Get the boring parts right and the rest is just a room you'll be oddly fond of later.
